text: Ἐπινοητικὴν οἶδε τὴν νοερὰν τῆς ψυχῆς δύναμιν. Expositio est ejus quod dixerat superiori, c. 100 τὴν τῶν ἡδέων ἐπινοητικὴν σχέσιν : sic passim, aliam alia sententia Maximus exponit, ac si esset diversus auctor. Esseque non raro suadeat Photii ipsa censura, a limine Quæst. ad Thalassium posita, et quod ipse quandoque deprehendi, Marci quædam αὐτολεξεὶ inserta aliis Maximi Capita. Refert ergo illud, οἶδε, superiorem auctorem, qui sic intellectum aut rationem, facultatem animi ἐπινοητικὴν (id est, excogitandi seu inveniendi solertem) quasi paraphrasi vocaverit, non divinam Scripturam aut sermonem, ut non bene reddidit Picus. Socus cum additur λόγος, uti quandoque facit Maximus, ac passim alii theologi.
anchorLine: ναμιν (l)· ἥτις χωριζομένη τῆς κατ' αἴσθησιν σχέ-
en: "He knows the inventive, intellectual power of the soul." This explains what was said in the preceding chapter (ch. 100), 'the inventive relation of pleasures'; Maximus often explains one thing by another, as if he were a different author. Photius's own censure, set at the head of the Quaestiones ad Thalassium, also suggests it, and that he himself has sometimes found passages of Mark inserted verbatim among other chapters of Maximus. So 'he knows' refers to the earlier author who, as if by paraphrase, called the intellect or reason, the faculty of the soul that is ἐπινοητική (that is, skilled at devising or inventing), not the divine Scripture or the Word, as Picus wrongly rendered it. [The word 'Socus' (probably a misprint for 'Secus' or 'Sic'), when λόγος is added, as Maximus sometimes does and other theologians often do.]

text: Ἡ ἄρρητος περιχώρησις τοῦ πεπιστευμένου. Alia profano usu hujus vocis significatio, quam hic conveniat. Quod vero reddit Picus, arcana processio, non satisfacit ; nec satis video quid ea voce velit. Budæus longe doctior in Damasceno de Trinit. divinam personarum περιχώρησιν, unionem reddit ; quod forte paulo liberius est : theologi circumincessionem vocant, quasi unius personæ in aliam undique immeationem ; malim ego, quod una capiat aliam ac velut contineat et comprehendat ; quomodo etiam dicuntur divinæ personæ ἀνεκφοιτήτως procedere, ita ut alia extra aliam non excedant : quæ vocis χωρεῖν, trita admodum significatio est, soletque et ad animum transferri, quod ille quasi continendo ac in se rem habendo, intelligat. Sic ergo Maximum intelligo. Manifestationem ac revelationem rei creditæ ac Dei (quæ fit per dona Spiritus adjuvantia fidem) ejus in nobis comprehensionem esse ac perceptionem : ut hinc in nobis habitantem habeamus ipsumque præsentem ac nobis intimum cognoscamus, juxta illud Pauli (Ephes. iii, 17) : Habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris. Nec istud vetat aliquid arcanam unionem dicere, et quasi commistionem, juxta quod Hesych. περιχωρεῖ, συμμίγεται exponit. Sed in his balbutimus, etsi Græci paulo nobis vocibus sunt feliciores. In aliis, nihil fere Picus felicior, ut quod ἀκίνητος στάσις, illi est, conditio semper movens ; non quia jugi incitata motu ; qualis fruentium Deo.
anchorLine: ἐκάστῳ πίστεως ἄρρητος τοῦ πεπιστευμένου (n)
en: "The ineffable perichoresis of what is believed." The word has another meaning than in profane use, one that suits this place. Picus's 'arcane procession' does not satisfy, and I do not quite see what he means by the word. Budaeus, a far better scholar, in his work on Damascene on the Trinity renders the divine perichoresis of the persons as 'union', which is perhaps a little free; theologians call it 'circumincession', as if one person's immeation into another all round; I would rather say it is that one takes in the other and as it were contains and comprehends it, as the divine persons are also said to proceed without going out, so that one does not go beyond the other; for the common sense of χωρεῖν is also carried over to the mind, because it understands by containing and holding the thing in itself. So I understand Maximus: the manifestation or revelation of the believed thing and of God (which comes about through the gifts of the Spirit that aid faith) is its comprehension and perception in us, so that we may have it dwelling in us, present, and know it intimately, as in Paul's word (Eph. iii, 17): 'that Christ dwell in your hearts by faith.' Nor does this forbid calling it a secret union and as it were a mixing, as Hesychius explains περιχωρεῖ by 'mixes'. But in these matters we stammer, though the Greeks are somewhat better supplied with words. In other places Picus is hardly happier, as when he renders ἀκίνητος στάσις 'a condition ever moving'; not [as] one impelled by continual motion; such is the state of those enjoying God.

text: Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν. Nulla hic commodius voce reddi videatur, quam si intentionalem dicamus ; quasi in animi rationibus et apprehensione positam ; quam et abstractivam rudiori vocabulo nostri theologi vocant. Affinis usus illius vocis Patribus vii synodi, dum adorationem imaginum, quam sanciunt, σχετικὴν vocant ; quæ scilicet non ad ipsam rem, ut in se est, terminatur, sed ut in sui similitudine, animo cogitanti quasi præsens objicitur, ac quadam in eam intentione ac motu, secundum quam dicitur honor imaginis transire ad exemp[l]ar seu prototypum. Nihil ad rem, quod Picus semel et iterum reconditam. Ac certe longe inaudi­tum mundo, quod quis ex ejus interpretamentis conficeret vocabularium : sic sine judicio cuncta viro arbitraria ; ut quod hic, ἡ μεθέξει κατ' ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις, illi cognitio est particeps operationis : quod ἔφεσιν, pro αἴσθησιν decoquit, etc.
anchorLine: τὴν μὲν σχετικὴν (ο), ὡς ἂν λόγῳ μόνῳ κειμένην
en: "The relational [knowledge]." No word seems more fitting than to call it 'intentional', as if placed in the soul's concepts and apprehension, which our theologians also call, in cruder vocabulary, 'abstractive'. The Fathers of the Seventh Council use the word similarly when they call the veneration of images that they sanction 'relational' (σχετική): it does not end in the thing itself as it is in itself, but as in its likeness it is presented as if present to the one thinking of it, with a certain intention and movement toward it, by which the honour of the image is said to pass to the exemplar or prototype. It is irrelevant that Picus (rendered it) 'hidden' time and again. But certainly it was unheard of in the world that anyone should compile a vocabulary from his renderings: thus everything, without judgement, becomes arbitrary for the man; as here, 'knowledge by participation in act' becomes 'a cognition that is partaker of operation'; and he boils ἔφεσιν down to αἴσθησιν, etc.

text: Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως. Quod semel et iterum cavet Maximus, hoc et 39 cap. ne τὸ ἀναιτίως et ἀναίτιον, quasi innoxium et sine culpa accipiatur, quæ est proclivis ejus vocis acceptio, id vero propense Picus amplectitur, ac ubique interpretatur. Est certe hæc voluptas eo sensu haud ἀναίτιος, sed culpæ conjuncta, et ex culpa, ni magis ipsa culpa ; ipse naturæ reatus ex transgressione, sic quasi brutæ vitæ, quæ libidine ducatur, nec jam ratione, sed magis sensu vivat : ἀναίτιος vero, id est sine causa, quod laborem, cui succedat, ejusque causa sit, nullum habeat. Unde nec Christus sic ἀναίτιον nativitatem ex libidine assumpsit, quod non illo modo ἀναίτιος, sed illi comitem laborem, exque illa, ὡς αἰτίας, ut eo juste, cum in illo injustus esset, nullo scilicet in ipso reatu, illam aboleret. Quam belle cohæret, ut Maximo ἀδικωτάτη, injustissima, sit hæc voluptas seu libido, et tamen ipsa ἀναίτιος sit, ipsa sine culpa, bello interprete Pico ? Nec enim ut labor injustus, sic et voluptas : quod hæc a voluntate existat, ille ab exteriore agente.
anchorLine: προκαθηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως (p). Ἀναίτιον δὲ φημι
en: "Without cause he led the way before the birth." Maximus guards, here and again in ch. 39, against ἀναιτίως and ἀναίτιον being taken as 'harmless and without fault', which is the easy meaning of the word; Picus eagerly adopts it and renders it so everywhere. This pleasure is certainly not 'blameless' in that sense but joined to fault and arising from fault, indeed more nearly itself the fault; the nature's guilt arises from transgression, as if of a brute life led by lust and no longer by reason, living rather by sense. But ἀναίτιος means 'without cause', in that it has no labour that follows it and of which it is the cause. Hence Christ did not take birth from lust as 'blameless' in that way, but with it a labour as companion, and from it, as from a cause, he justly abolished it, being himself unjust in it [sic; i.e. not unjust], with no guilt in himself. How well it coheres, that for Maximus it is ἀδικωτάτη, 'most unjust', this pleasure or lust, and yet is ἀναίτιος, 'without fault', as Picus nicely renders it? For it is not as with labour, unjust; so also with pleasure: this arises from the will, that from an external agent.

text: Τῆς ἀπαθοῦς φύσεως. Sic dicta in Christo natura, sicque repræsentant codd. atque edita, cui proinde labor atque mors, ἄδικος ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀναίτιος foret. Sed mihi istud durius : longe vero expeditius ; quod habetur, Quæst. ad Thal. πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς παθούσης φύσεως : quod et reddidi. Sic certe tota laborabat natura, totaque reparanda, Christi laboribus et morte non naturæ ἀπαθοῦς, quod nec ipsa sic absolute dicatur Christi natura, quæ τὸ παθητὸν carnis haberet, quantumvis esset ἀπαθής, quod ad vitium attinet ac culpam.
anchorLine: πρὸς δὲ τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς ἀπαθοῦς φύσεως (q),
en: "Of the impassible nature." So the nature is called in Christ, and so the manuscripts and the printed text give it, so that labour and death would for it be 'unjust and also without cause'. But to me that is harder; far easier is what is read in the Quaestiones ad Thalassium, 'for the repair of the suffering nature' (πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς παθούσης φύσεως), which I have also rendered. Certainly the whole nature laboured and the whole needed repair, by Christ's labours and death, and not the nature [as] impassible, since not even Christ's nature is so called absolutely, which had the capacity to suffer (τὸ παθητόν) of flesh, although it was impassible (ἀπαθής) as regards vice and guilt. (The editor proposes/prefers παθούσης; the note spans both columns.)

text: Οἱ μὲν τῇ φύσει. Quod sic hic, et sequenti cap. ac passim alibi Maximus naturam ingerit, ejusque rationem ut virtutis omnis regulam, ac necessitudinis cum Deo normam ; ut tantum Deo uniamur ac virtute fulgeamus, simusque capaces æternæ beatitudinis, quantum nobis ac nostræ vo- [continues on p-0678: luntati cum naturæ rationibus convenerit ; de natura sanata et instituta per gratiam, omnino intelligendum non de ipsa quatenus in nobis ex transgressione pro peccato inolevit : de natura demum qualis a Deo condita fuit, imagine ornata et similitudine, in qua divini elucerent characteres, non cui obducta ex peccato brutorum ipsa πάθη (libidines scilicet), virtutis cultu ac exercitatione a nobis excutienda, ut divina in nobis instauretur vita, quod non aliter habemus, quam Christi gratia.]
anchorLine: νδʹ. Οἱ μὲν τῇ φύσει (r) φυλάξαντες διὰ πάντων
en: "Those who by nature [...]." As here and in the following chapter, and in many other places, Maximus brings in nature and its principle as the rule of all virtue and the norm of kinship with God, so that we may be united to God and shine in virtue, and be capable of eternal blessedness in proportion as it falls to us and our will agrees with the principles of nature. [The text must be understood] of nature healed and restored through grace, not of nature as, through transgression, it has grown in us by sin; but of nature as it was created by God, adorned with the image and likeness in which the divine characteristics shone, not that upon which the brutish passions (that is, lusts) have been laid by sin, to be cast out by us through the practice and exercise of virtue, that divine life may be restored in us, which we have in no other way than by the grace of Christ.

text: Τὸ ἐν ἐπ' αὐτοῦ. Legit Picus ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, ac reddere conatus est, Pie sub se habet unum, quod est et dicitur. Quod sane sensum habet absurdissimum, ac si velit Christum superius prædicatum esse, sub quo unum et sit et intelligatur. Ait itaque Maximus, unum pie semper in Christo et de Christo esse et intelligi, ea ratione qua persona est, nullamque distinctionem admittit. Deinde ὑπ' αὐτὸν legendum foret, quod nec ipse repræsentat Picus.
anchorLine: κατὰ πάντα τρόπον τὸ ἓν ἐπ' αὐτοῦ (s) διαπαντὸς
en: "The one on him." Picus read ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ('under him') and tried to render it 'piously has under itself the one, which is and is said'. That makes a most absurd sense, as if he meant Christ were spoken of above, under whom the one both is and is understood. Maximus therefore says that the one is always piously in Christ and of Christ and is understood, in that he is a person, and admits no distinction. Further, ὑπ' αὐτὸν would have to be read, which Picus himself does not represent. (The editor reports Picus's variant ὑπ' αὐτοῦ and prefers ἐπ' αὐτοῦ as the text.)
